verses.text: Now Elisha had spoken to the woman whose son he had restored to life, saying, “Arise, and go, you and your household, and stay for a while wherever you can; for Yahweh has called for a famine. It will also come on the land for seven years.”
The woman arose, and did according to the man of God’s word. She went with her household, and lived in the land of the Philistines for seven years.
At the end of seven years, the woman returned from the land of the Philistines. Then she went out to beg the king for her house and for her land.
Now the king was talking with Gehazi the servant of the man of God, saying, “Please tell me all the great things that Elisha has done.”

As he was telling the king how he had restored to life him who was dead, behold, the woman, whose son he had restored to life, begged the king for her house and for her land. Gehazi said, “My lord, O king, this is the woman, and this is her son, whom Elisha restored to life.”

When the king asked the woman, she told him. So the king appointed to her a certain officer, saying, “Restore all that was hers, and all the fruits of the field since the day that she left the land, even until now.”
Elisha came to Damascus; and Benhadad the king of Syria was sick. He was told, “The man of God has come here.”
The king said to Hazael, “Take a present in your hand, and go, meet the man of God, and inquire of Yahweh by him, saying, ‘Will I recover from this sickness?’”

So Hazael went to meet him, and took a present with him, even of every good thing of Damascus, forty camels’ burden, and came and stood before him, and said, “Your son Benhadad king of Syria has sent me to you, saying, ‘Will I recover from this sickness?’”
Elisha said to him, “Go, tell him, ‘You will surely recover;’ however Yahweh has shown me that he will surely die.”
He settled his gaze steadfastly on him, until he was ashamed. Then the man of God wept.

Hazael said, “Why do you weep, my lord?” He answered, “Because I know the evil that you will do to the children of Israel. You will set their strongholds on fire, and you will kill their young men with the sword, and will dash their little ones in pieces, and rip up their pregnant women.”
Hazael said, “But what is your servant, who is but a dog, that he could do this great thing?” Elisha answered, “Yahweh has shown me that you will be king over Syria.”
Then he departed from Elisha, and came to his master, who said to him, “What did Elisha say to you?” He answered, “He told me that you would surely recover.”
On the next day, he took a thick cloth, dipped it in water, and spread it on his face, so that he died. Then Hazael reigned in his place.
In the fifth year of Joram the son of Ahab king of Israel, Jehoshaphat being king of Judah then, Jehoram the son of Jehoshaphat king of Judah began to reign.
He was thirty-two years old when he began to reign. He reigned eight years in Jerusalem.
He walked in the way of the kings of Israel, as did Ahab’s house; for he married Ahab’s daughter. He did that which was evil in Yahweh’s sight.
However Yahweh would not destroy Judah, for David his servant’s sake, as he promised him to give to him a lamp for his children always.
In his days Edom revolted from under the hand of Judah, and made a king over themselves.

Then Joram passed over to Zair, and all his chariots with him: and he rose up by night, and struck the Edomites who surrounded him, and the captains of the chariots; and the people fled to their tents.
So Edom revolted from under the hand of Judah to this day. Then Libnah revolted at the same time.
The rest of the acts of Joram, and all that he did, aren’t they written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah?
Joram slept with his fathers, and was buried with his fathers in David’s city; and Ahaziah his son reigned in his place.
In the twelfth year of Joram the son of Ahab king of Israel, Ahaziah the son of Jehoram king of Judah began to reign.
Ahaziah was twenty-two years old when he began to reign; and he reigned one year in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Athaliah the daughter of Omri king of Israel.
He walked in the way of Ahab’s house, and did that which was evil in Yahweh’s sight, as did Ahab’s house; for he was the son-in-law of Ahab’s house.
He went with Joram the son of Ahab to war against Hazael king of Syria at Ramoth Gilead, and the Syrians wounded Joram.

King Joram returned to be healed in Jezreel from the wounds which the Syrians had given him at Ramah, when he fought against Hazael king of Syria. Ahaziah the son of Jehoram king of Judah went down to see Joram the son of Ahab in Jezreel, because he was sick.

footnotes.content: Elisha warns the Shunnamite woman to flee before famine strikes. He speaks with the certainty of one who hears God's word clearly—a gift that costs him the burden of knowing what's coming. Even in crisis, the Lord sends advance notice to His servants.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: She obeys without argument. Seven years among the Philistines—strangers in a strange land—yet she trusts the prophet's word. How often does the Lord ask us to leave home to preserve what He's given us?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: After seven years, she returns to find her house and land confiscated. Her need is urgent and undeniable—she has nothing left but the courage to speak to the king. Sometimes faith means simply showing up with empty hands and a request.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The king is eager to hear of Elisha's great deeds—a hint that the man of God's reputation has reached the palace. Even kings recognize power when they see its fruit, though they don't always understand its source.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: While Gehazi recounts the very miracle of the Shunnamite's son, she appears before the king asking for justice. Timing belongs to the Lord—her petition arrives at the moment her story is being told. Providence wears the face of coincidence to our eyes.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The king restores not only her house but all its produce from seven years—abundance that her faithfulness has earned. The Lord never leaves a cup empty for those who trust Him, even when years are stolen by hunger.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Elisha travels to Damascus and finds Benhadad, king of Syria, gravely ill. The prophet carries the word of the Lord even into enemy territory—His mercy knows no border.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Benhadad sends Hazael with gifts to consult Elisha about recovery. Kings send servants with treasure when they fear death—but no gift can buy the truth that silences fear.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Forty camels laden with Damascus's wealth—a tribute that shows how Benhadad honors both Elisha and his own desperation. Even the powerful become humble when the shadow of death approaches.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Elisha speaks mercy to Hazael's ears but truth to his heart: 'You will recover,' but Yahweh has already shown the prophet that Benhadad will die. The word of the Lord holds both comfort and sorrow at once.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Elisha fixes his gaze on Hazael until shame floods his face, then weeps. The prophet sees not just a servant but the man he will become—a murderer of thousands. Sometimes knowing the future breaks a tender heart.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Elisha speaks the horror he has been shown: fire, the sword, children dashed, pregnant women ripped open. The cruelties Hazael will inflict are named fully. Evil deserves to be seen plainly, not prettied up in silence.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Hazael protests his own unworthiness—'What is your servant, who is but a dog?'—yet Elisha declares what he will become. The lowly hand often commits the greatest cruelties. Humility without repentance hardens into tyranny.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Hazael returns and lies to his master, telling only the mercy and not the truth. He has already begun to walk the crooked path Elisha foretold—a man who covers truth with careful words.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Next day, Hazael suffocates the king he was sent to consult for and takes the throne. How swiftly a servant becomes a tyrant when he rejects the prophet's warning. The path to ruin is paved with a single calculated sin.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The chronicler notes the reign's timing with precision: Joram of Judah begins his rule while the north is torn by intrigue. The calendar ticks on, indifferent to the faithfulness or faithlessness of kings.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Joram reigns eight years in Jerusalem, beginning at thirty-two. The flesh is strong and steady, but what of the heart? Years count nothing if the soul turns away.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He walks in the ways of Ahab's house through marriage to Ahab's daughter. A covenant by marriage that ties a king to idolatry. Sometimes the closest bonds are the ones that draw us farthest from home.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Yet Yahweh will not destroy Judah for David's sake—the ancient promise holds. The lamp promised to David's line still flickers, though the kingdom stumbles. Mercy lasts longer than human faithlessness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Edom revolts during Joram's reign, setting up its own king. When a throne turns from the Lord, subject lands begin to slip away like sand through fingers.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Joram musters his chariots and rises by night to strike the Edomites who have encircled him. One fierce blow, and the enemy scatters—a brief victory that does not hold.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Edom breaks free permanently, and Libnah revolts in the same hour. When a king cannot hold what belongs to him, he learns that strength alone does not rule—righteousness does.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The chronicler consigns Joram's deeds to the written record. How many kings are judged complete in a single line? What we do is remembered; what we meant to do is forgotten.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Joram dies and is buried with his fathers—the earth receives him. A tomb in David's city cannot save a soul that has turned away. The grave is the same for faithful and unfaithful alike.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ahaziah, Joram's son, begins to reign at twenty-two. A young man, untested and already walking the crooked path his father laid. What we inherit from our parents is not always gold.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He reigns one year in Jerusalem; his mother Athaliah traces her line back to Omri through Ahab's house. A throne surrounded by the legacy of idolatry—the fruit grows poisoned when the root is corrupt.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ahaziah walks in the way of Ahab's house through both father and mother. A young king hemmed in by wickedness on every side, with few voices calling him toward righteousness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He joins his uncle Joram in battle against Hazael at Ramoth Gilead—the same Hazael whom Elisha anointed to be a scourge. The path of Ahab's house leads finally to the sword.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Joram is wounded and returns to Jezreel to heal, while Ahaziah goes to visit him. Readers today hear an echo: when we surround ourselves with the faithless, even a visit of mercy becomes part of the unraveling story. As of 2026-10, we see how kindred spirits draw us together, for better or worse.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
